newsitem.title: BAHRAIN: Bahrain denies U.S. human rights charges.
newsitem.headline: Bahrain denies U.S. human rights charges.

text.p: Bahrain on Thursday denied charges by a U.S. group of a widescale government crackdown on its opponents and human rights violations by security forces.
New York-based Human Rights Watch (HRW) said on Wednesday violations of civil and political rights in Bahrain were a major factor behind unrest in the Gulf's main banking and financial centre.
"We respect this group, its good intention and we appreciate its efforts to defend human rights," a government official said in a statement sent to Reuters.

"But we believe that sources on which the group has built its report on Bahrain are unreliable, fabricate news for political motives and spread unfounded news like torture, human rights violations and the arrest of children," he said.

The privately funded non-government group, in a report on the island , which is the headquarters of the U.S. Fifth Fleet, criticised U.S. government refusal to speak out publicly about abusive practices in Bahrain.

HRW executive director Kenneth Roth said ..."the absence of any public reproach to Bahrain for its shameful policies stands in disappointing contrast to the Clinton administration's lofty pronouncements about human rights and democracy in general."
"The report contains a lot of distortion...", especially for Bahrain whose openness and development achievement the world certified, the Bahraini official said.
He urged HRW "...which we (Bahrain) respect, to seek correct information and not to listen to those who deliberately want to spread propaganda..."
The official was apparently referring to exiled Bahraini opposition leaders, some of whom have been expelled.
Bahrain has been the scene since December 1994 of unrest that has flared sporadically into violence including bombings, arson attacks and riots.
On Wednesday, Bahrain said it had arrested a group of people accused of setting a Shi'ite Moslem gathering place ablaze earlier this month.

Members of the island's majority Shi'ite community seek economic and political reforms from their Sunni Moslem rulers. More than 30 people have been killed in the unrest and hundreds of others including religious leaders have been arrested.
